title: Four Ways of Not Really Doing It
core: All four describe something that technically happened but didn't amount to much — the motions were gone through, the substance wasn't. The event is never denied; what's denied is depth, care, or weight. They differ by *which* thing went missing: time, interest, depth, or sincerity. Three are quiet accusations aimed at the doer; one can be purely descriptive.

words.nuance: The failure is **speed**. A cursory look was too fast to catch what a slower one would have — the implied fix is more time. It clings to acts of perception (glance, reading, inspection); you can't give a cursory donation.

The failure is **motive**, not pace. A perfunctory ritual can be slow, complete, and correctly performed — it's dead inside, done because duty demanded it. This is the one that says the person didn't care, regardless of how much of the task got finished.

The only one that measures **depth reached** rather than judging the doer, and the only one with a genuinely neutral sense: a superficial wound is good news. Figuratively it faults an analysis for stopping at appearances — it says nothing about whether that was haste, indifference, or plain inability.

The only one where the smallness is **deliberate and aimed at an audience** — done precisely so it can be pointed at later. A token raise isn't a lapse of care; it's a calculated purchase of the appearance of compliance. Also the group's only noun, and there the tone flips warm: a token of affection.

exam_note: Sentence Equivalence loves pairing **cursory** with **perfunctory** as if they were the twin answer — check whether the sentence blames the clock (cursory) or the attitude (perfunctory); and don't reject **superficial** just because the context is a literal, non-insulting wound or crack.
